name: Scrub Typhus

pathogens.why: Orientia tsutsugamushi is the sole cause of scrub typhus; the clinical diagnosis (eschar, lymphadenopathy, exposure history in an endemic rural/peri-urban setting) is often sufficiently characteristic to justify empiric treatment before serology returns.

investigations.why: Eschar (a painless, often overlooked necrotic lesion at the chigger bite site) is highly specific for scrub typhus when found - actively look in skin folds, axillae, groin.

investigations.test: Scrub typhus IgM ELISA / Weil-Felix (less specific)
investigations.why: Confirms diagnosis serologically, though treatment should not wait for results when clinical suspicion is high.
Assesses organ involvement; transaminitis and thrombocytopenia are common supportive findings.
Screens for ARDS, a recognized complication of severe/delayed scrub typhus.

references: NCDC India Guidelines for Rickettsial Diseases
reason: is consistent with scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi infection) - a rickettsial illness that is readily treatable with antibiotics but can progress to multi-organ dysfunction (ARDS, myocarditis, encephalitis) if treatment is delayed. Empiric doxycycline should be started promptly on clinical suspicion without waiting for serology confirmation, given the excellent response to early treatment and the risk of severe disease with delay.

clinicalPearls: The classic triad of an inoculation eschar at the chigger feeding site, regional lymphadenopathy, and a maculopapular rash is the textbook description, but these signs are seldom seen in indigenous (local endemic) patients (Harrison 22e p.1460).
Among returning travelers, fewer than 50% develop an eschar and fewer than 40% develop a rash; when a rash does appear it typically emerges on day 4-6 of illness (Harrison 22e p.1460).

Eschar formation occurs at the site of mite/chigger feeding and may develop during the incubation period; an eschar is a useful diagnostic clue that should prompt consideration of scrub typhus (Harrison 22e p.1455).

Onset after a 6-21 day incubation is characterized by fever, headache, myalgia, cough, and gastrointestinal symptoms; some patients recover spontaneously after a few days while others progress to severe disease (Harrison 22e p.1460).
Chigger bites may be asymptomatic, so the absence of a recalled bite does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.3773).

Immunity to scrub typhus is short-lived: protection against the homologous strain wanes over 1-3 years, and the organism's marked antigenic diversity means cross-protective immunity can be lost in as little as 1 month, so reinfection is possible (Harrison 22e p.1460).
harrison.pathophysiology: Scrub typhus is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi, an obligate intracellular organism placed in a separate genus within the family Rickettsiaceae. It differs substantially from Rickettsia species both genetically and in cell-wall composition, notably lacking lipopolysaccharide. Disease results from infection of vascular endothelial cells with increased vascular permeability (a mechanism shared across the rickettsioses). The organism is maintained in nature by transovarial transmission within trombiculid mites; infected larval mites (chiggers, the only mite stage that feeds on a vertebrate host) inoculate the organism into the skin during feeding. Severe disease reflects widespread vascular injury, producing the encephalitis and interstitial pneumonia that characterize advanced cases. Closely related Orientia species (O. chuto, Candidatus O. chiloensis) cause scrub typhus-like illness in newly recognized foci (Harrison 22e p.1455-1456, p.1460, p.3773).
infectionMimics: Other rickettsioses presenting with eschar, rash, fever and headache (e.g., Mediterranean spotted fever, African tick-bite fever, rickettsialpox, murine and epidemic typhus) (Harrison 22e p.1455-1456).
Atypical/community-acquired pneumonia, given the cough and dyspnea of pulmonary involvement (Harrison 22e p.1126).
Other undifferentiated tropical febrile illnesses with thrombocytopenia and transaminitis.
additionalInvestigations: Serology is the mainstay of laboratory diagnosis: indirect fluorescent antibody, indirect immunoperoxidase, enzyme immunoassays, and rapid lateral-flow chromatographic tests (Harrison 22e p.1460).
PCR amplification of Orientia genes is effective when performed on eschar material, but is less sensitive on blood (Harrison 22e p.1460).
Platelet count: thrombocytopenia is a characteristic laboratory finding in scrub typhus (as in other rickettsioses) (Harrison 22e p.1455).
WBC count is typically normal or low (Harrison 22e p.1455).
Serum sodium: hyponatremia is a recognized associated finding across the rickettsioses (Harrison 22e p.1455).
Hepatic aminotransferases: mild to moderate elevation is commonly seen (Harrison 22e p.1455).
redFlags: Altered mental status / encephalitis (meningoencephalitis is a feature of severe disease) (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1455).
Interstitial pneumonia / pneumonitis with dyspnea or progression toward respiratory failure (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1460).
Signs of disseminated intravascular coagulation or hemorrhage (Harrison 22e p.1035).
Progressive hypotension and multiorgan failure (a severe-disease pattern shared by the rickettsioses) (Harrison 22e p.1455).
harrison.prognosis: Illness ranges from mild and self-limiting to fatal. The case-fatality rate for untreated classic cases is about 6% and would likely be lower if all mild cases were captured; overall reported mortality varies widely by location (cited as 1% to 70%). Risk of death rises with increasing age and with the presence of myocarditis, delirium, pneumonitis, or signs of hemorrhage. Recognized in time, the disease responds well to appropriate antibiotic therapy (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1460).
pitfalls: Relying on the classic triad: eschar, rash, and lymphadenopathy are frequently absent (eschar <50% and rash <40% of travelers; signs seldom seen in indigenous patients), so a negative skin exam does not exclude scrub typhus (Harrison 22e p.1460).
Expecting a recalled bite: chigger bites may be asymptomatic and the mites are tiny and rarely noticed (Harrison 22e p.3773).

Assuming geographic exclusion: although classically eastern/southern Asia, northern Australia, and Pacific/Indian Ocean islands, emerging and reemerging foci (e.g., Chile, parts of South/Central America, Africa, Arabian peninsula via related Orientia species) challenge the traditional epidemiology (Harrison 22e p.1460, p.3773).
Note that PCR on blood is less sensitive than PCR on eschar material (Harrison 22e p.1460).
Some Thai isolates are poorly responsive to doxycycline or chloramphenicol (Harrison 22e p.1460).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison does not give a formal severity score; it contrasts mild/self-limiting illness with severe disease. Severe scrub typhus is marked by encephalitis/meningoencephalitis and interstitial pneumonia due to vascular injury, and may progress to myocarditis, DIC, renal failure, hypotension, and multiorgan failure (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1455, p.1460).
